dedupe_keys.name: gannon storm gnss degradation and midwest corn production losses may 2024

description: This post-event analysis estimates the farm losses caused when the extreme G5 geomagnetic storm of 10 to 13 May 2024, named the Gannon storm, degraded satellite positioning at the peak of corn planting in the US Midwest. Real-time kinematic correction services used by automatically steered tractors from John Deere and other makers delivered poor corrections, and many farmers stopped planting from the afternoon of 10 May for up to two days, at a time when planting was already late because of wet weather. Griffin, Knipp, Shank, Mulligan Skov, McIntosh and Leamon built a representative-farm model from USDA statistics and extension publications, with space-weather data from GFZ Potsdam and the NOAA Space Weather Prediction Center, and estimated foregone revenue of $12,000 to $17,000 for a GNSS-reliant Illinois farm and foregone production of 17.4 million to 424 million bushels, worth about $69.6 million to $1.7 billion, across twelve Midwestern states. Coverage: twelve US Midwestern states, May 2024. Format and access: free working paper on AgManager.info (5 March 2025) with a Zenodo DOI, 10.5281/zenodo.14976490. Caveats: the share of affected farms and the yield penalty for late planting are assumptions, so the range is wide; losses in other sectors are not covered. Simulation uses: hazard exposure of GNSS-dependent services to space weather, cascading effects from positioning into agriculture, and loss functions for space-weather risk assessments. Related records: the Arctic scintillation data from the same storm, IGS products and the NOAA CORS network describe the signal effects, and the Starlink loss of February 2022 is another space-weather case.
